sentences.text: Sebecus is an extinct genus of terrestrial, carnivorous crocodylomorph that lived in South America during the Paleogene period.
The genus Sebecus currently includes two valid species: the type species S. icaeorhinus and S. ayrampu.
Unlike modern crocodilians, Sebecus possessed a deep and narrow snout, a feature that distinguishes it from other crocodilomorphs.
The name Sebecus is a Latinization of Sebek, also called Sobek, the crocodile god of ancient Egypt.
The species name icaeorhinus derives from Greek words meaning 'chance' or 'not according to plan' and 'snout', referring to the animal's unusually deep snout.
The nostrils of Sebecus were located at the very tip of its snout.
Postcranial remains suggest Sebecus had a total body length of 2.2 to 3.1 meters and weighed between 52.2 and 113.5 kilograms.
The animal featured unusual ziphodont dentition characterized by teeth that were laterally compressed and serrated.
Ultrastructural analysis using electron microscopes revealed micro-scratches on Sebecus teeth suggesting a specific method of cutting meat.
American paleontologist George Gaylord Simpson named the genus Sebecus in 1937, making it one of the earliest known sebecosuchians.
Simpson described the type species S. icaeorhinus based on a fragmented skull and lower jaw discovered in the Sarmiento Formation.
The rock layer containing a partial skull and jaw belongs to the Paleocene Mealla Formation.
The postcranial skeleton of S. icaeorhinus remained largely unknown until Pol et al. (2012) described remains including a partially articulated specimen MPEF-PV 1776.
Sebecus elements provided additional evidence of its terrestrial condition, as its legs, especially its femurs, were proportionally longer than those of modern crocodilians.
The Eustachian tubes in Sebecus were very complex, featuring several interconnected branches similar to those of crocodilians.
Colbert interpreted the small telencephalon of Sebecus as a sign of primitivism, suggesting an evolutionary trend toward larger brains in crocodilians.
Sebecus belongs to the family Sebecidae.

Sebecus has been placed in various positions within the group of metasuchian crocodyliforms, and recent phylogenetic analyses suggest Sebecosuchia is polyphyletic, with Sebecus forming a metasuchian clade distantly related to Notosuchia.
Colbert placed Sebecus and the Cretaceous Baurusuchus in the order Sebecosuchia because both possessed high, deep snouts and ziphodont teeth.
Sebecus has been used to define major groups of crocodilomorphs, including the family Sebecidae and the suborder Sebecosuchia.
Fossils of Sebecus range from the Paleocene to the Mid Eocene, with possible records extending to the Late Miocene or Early Pliocene.
Sebecus was an extinct sebecid crocodylomorph that lived during the Eocene in present-day Patagonia, South America.
The deposits date to the Laventense (about 12 million years old), extending the genus's temporal range in the Neogene by nearly 40 million years.
Sebecus lived from the Danian to the Zanclean epochs, approximately 66 to 3.6 million years ago.

A 2007 study reclassified S. huilensis and S. querejazus into separate genera, Zulmasuchus and Langstonia, respectively, a move also noted by Paolillo and Linares who assigned these species to new genera.
Larsson and Sues (2007) named the clade Sebecia to address conflicting phylogenetic placements of Sebecus.
